newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Divided Nicaragua prepares for new president.
newsitem.headline: Divided Nicaragua prepares for new president.

text.p: Right-wing President-elect Arnoldo Aleman takes power on Friday facing a bitter fight with left-wing Sandinistas and pressure to deal with Nicaragua's crushing poverty and unemployment.

In a ceremony billed as the consolidation of Nicaragua's fledgling democracy, Aleman will receive the presidential sash from President Violeta Chamorro, who ends nearly seven years in office that saw the end of an eight-year civil war and the return of capitalism.

Seven presidents, delegates from 61 countries and 22,000 spectators were expected to overrun Managua's Rigoberto Lopez Stadium to see the ceremony under the watchful eyes of 2,300 police officers and bomb-sniffing dogs, police said.

"For the first time in more than 100 years of Nicaraguan history, one civilian, democratically elected president will hand over power to another," boasted Chamorro, who leaves office with her popularity at its highest point ever.

Adding to the euphoria are signs of economic growth as Nicaragua emerges from economic collapse in the 1980s. The economy grew by 5.5 percent in 1996 and outgoing government officials have predicted up to 7 percent growth in 1997.
"After five years I can say with responsibility that we are an emerging country with a future and capacity to grow," outgoing Central Bank President Evenor Taboada said.
Nicaraguans have high hopes that Aleman, a 50-year-old lawyer and former mayor of the capital Managua, will deliver.

A CID-Gallup poll in December showed that 44 percent of Nicaraguans thought their economic situation would improve in 1997 compared to 24 percent who thought it would worsen. More than half thought Aleman would be either "very capable" or "capable" of resolving the country's problems.

But Aleman will face tough obstacles, analysts said. Seven years after the end of its civil war Nicaragua remains pauperised and bitterly polarised between Aleman's right-wing Liberal Alliance and the left-wing Sandinstas.
The United Nations ranks Nicaragua as the second poorest country in Latin America. More than 70 percent of its population live below the poverty line.

Aleman has promised to make creating jobs his government's top priority but he will face shrinking foreign aid and tough pressure to reduce the bloated state payroll, future Economy Minister Francisco Lainez told Reuters.
Also haunting Aleman is his archrivals the Sandinistas, who say his Oct. 20 election victory over Sandinista candidate and former President Daniel Ortega was fraudulent.
